text:
A city of rivers and bridges, of trams and schools.
The working day had just begun.

At 8:15, an American B-29 bomber, the Enola Gay,
released a single atomic bomb.

It exploded about 600 metres above the city.
In an instant, the heart of Hiroshima was gone.

In the months that followed, an estimated
90,000 to 166,000 people died.

Three days later, clouds hid the city of Kokura,
so a second bomber, Bockscar, turned toward Nagasaki.

At 11:02, a plutonium bomb exploded over the Urakami valley.
60,000 to 80,000 people died.

On 15 August, Japan announced its surrender. The war was over.
For the survivors, the hibakusha, it was not.

Sadako Sasaki was 2 years old when the bomb fell on Hiroshima.
At 12, sick with leukemia, she folded paper cranes, hoping to live.

After she died, her classmates raised a monument to her,
and to every child the bombs had taken.
The next spring, in the ashes, the oleander bloomed.

Every year at 8:15, Hiroshima falls silent.
And the survivors keep telling their story, so that it never happens again.
